introduction: These readings use one picture for the purpose of a human life: a tree is for its fruit. A tree may be tall and green and still be useless, and so a person’s faith, knowledge or spiritual experience is known by what it yields in love, trustworthiness and service to others. The readings press the point with seasons, since now is the time of fruit, with the echo that returns from a mountain, and with a long series of hopes that their readers will become fruitful trees. The picture is the Bible’s and the Qur’an’s as well, and the Gospel sayings on trees and their fruit stand beside the readings throughout. Other voices ask what the picture can hide: Kant and Milton hold that a good will or a patient waiting has its worth without results, the Gita asks for action with no eye on the fruit, Paul says that God gives the increase, and the Preacher doubts whether any labour leaves a profit.
questions: The readings say that a tree is judged by its fruit and not by its leaves. What are the leaves in a religious life, and what the fruit?

Kant thought a good will would shine like a jewel even if it achieved nothing, and Milton that they also serve who only stand and wait. How would you answer them from these readings, and what would you concede?

Krishna asks for right action without attachment to its fruit, and Marcus Aurelius admires the vine that seeks nothing more once it has borne. How can a person aim at results and not be ruled by them?
Paul says that one plants, another waters, and God gives the increase; Jesus that one sows and another reaps. What follows for how we count our own results?
Several readings say that now is the season. What would be different this month if you believed that?

outside.why: Jesus gave the test in the same picture: ye shall know them by their fruits.
Paul lists the fruit of the Spirit, and love stands first in the list.
Luke's Gospel says that a good man brings good out of the treasure of his heart, as a good tree brings good fruit.
The last vision of the Bible has a tree of life whose leaves are for the healing of the nations.
Jesus asks his critics to judge consistently: make the tree good and its fruit good, for the tree is known by its fruit.
Jesus calls himself the vine and his followers the branches, which bear nothing when they are cut off from it.
Jesus warned about teachers who come in sheep's clothing, and gave fruit as the way to tell them.
James makes the same challenge: show me thy faith without thy works, and I will show thee my faith by my works.

The letter to the Ephesians insists that salvation is by grace through faith, not of works, lest anyone boast. If results are the proof of what is spiritual, what keeps a person from trusting in the results?
Jesus says his Father is glorified when his disciples bear much fruit.
The first psalm likens the godly person to a tree planted by rivers of water that brings forth fruit in its season.
Marcus Aurelius admires the person who does good as a vine bears grapes and seeks nothing more afterwards. What becomes of the fruit when the tree keeps count of it?
The letter to Titus speaks of those who profess that they know God and in works deny Him.
Paul reminds the Corinthians of the farmer's rule: whoever sows sparingly reaps sparingly.
Jesus came to a fig tree in full leaf, found nothing on it but leaves, and it withered.
The Qur’an likens a good word to a good tree, firmly rooted, giving its fruit at every season.
Jesus told his disciples not to say that harvest was four months away: the fields were already white.
Jeremiah gives the cry of those for whom the season went by: the harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved. What makes a person let a time of fruit pass?
The Preacher advises sowing in the morning and not holding back in the evening, since no one knows which will prosper.
Jesus says that the work must be done while it is day, for the night comes when no one can work.
Longfellow's Psalm of Life ends with the same counsel: let us be up and doing, with a heart for any fate.
In the parable the owner has come three years seeking fruit on his fig tree, and the gardener asks for one year more.
Shakespeare looks at his own late season, with yellow leaves or none upon the boughs. What can be asked of a person in whom the spring is over?
The psalm asks to be taught to number our days, so that we may apply our hearts to wisdom.
John the Baptist used the same severity: the axe is laid to the root, and every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down.
Milton, blind and unable to use his one talent, concluded that God does not need man's work, and that they also serve who only stand and wait. Is there a fruit that cannot be seen from outside?
Kant held that a good will which achieved nothing would still shine like a jewel, and that its fruitfulness can add nothing to its worth. Is a life to be valued by its results or by its intention?
Isaiah sings of a vineyard that was given every care and brought forth wild grapes.
Jesus says that the branch which bears no fruit is taken away, and the one that bears is pruned to bear more.
The letter of Jude speaks of trees whose fruit withers, twice dead and plucked up by the roots.
Ben Jonson said it of a short life: in small proportions we just beauties see, and in short measures life may perfect be.
George Eliot thought the growing good of the world depends on unhistoric acts and on lives that rest in unvisited tombs. How would anyone know whether such a life was fruitful?
Jesus tells his disciples that he chose them and appointed them to bring forth fruit that should remain.
The seer of Revelation sees the books opened and the dead judged according to their works.
In the parable of the sower some seed fell on good ground and yielded a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.
The Qur’an says that whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it.
Paul states the law of the echo in the farmer's terms: whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
Hosea gives the dark side of the same law: they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind.
Jesus advises laying up treasure where moth and rust do not corrupt.
Shelley's king left a trace too: a boast on a pedestal in an empty desert. What distinguishes the trace this reading means from the monument that Ozymandias built?
The Preacher says: cast thy bread upon the waters, for thou shalt find it after many days.
The Preacher looked back on all that his hands had made, and found it vanity and no profit under the sun. What would he need to hear to believe that a life's labour can yield anything lasting?
The psalm promises that those planted in the house of the Lord shall still bring forth fruit in old age.
The Qur’an says that a person has only that for which he makes effort.
Isaiah's servant says: I have laboured in vain, I have spent my strength for nought; yet surely my judgment is with the Lord. How does someone who works hard and sees no success keep working?
Paul says: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase, so that neither planter nor waterer is anything. Whose are the fruits of a life?
Jesus asks that people see his followers' good works and give the glory to their Father.
James warns against hearing the word and not doing it, like a man who looks in a mirror and forgets his face.
Hosea calls on his people to sow in righteousness, reap in mercy, and break up their fallow ground.
Jeremiah's tree by the waters does not fear the heat or the year of drought, and never ceases to yield fruit.
The Qur’an likens what is spent in God's way to a grain that grows seven ears, with a hundred grains in each.
Paul hopes that the Philippians will shine as lights in the world.
In the parable of the talents each servant receives according to his ability, and is asked what he made of it.
The Qur’an recalls the Gospel's likeness of sown corn that sends out its shoot, strengthens it and stands firm on its stalk.
Hopkins, seeing everything else in leaf, prays: mine, O thou lord of life, send my roots rain.
Mencius tells of a man who pulled at his corn to help it grow and came home to find it withered. What part of growth can be hastened by wishing, and what must be left to its time?
Hosea hears a promise: I will be as the dew, and he shall grow as the lily and cast forth his roots.
Proverbs says that the fruit of the righteous is a tree of life.
Habakkuk says that though the fig tree should not blossom and no fruit be on the vines, yet he will rejoice. What remains of faith in a season that yields nothing?
Jesus said of the teachers of his day: do not after their works, for they say and do not.
The Dhammapada compares fine words that are not acted on to a beautiful flower without scent.
Paul prays that the Colossians may be fruitful in every good work and increase in the knowledge of God.
Jesus quotes a saying: one soweth, and another reapeth. What does it ask of a person to work for a result that others will gather?
Krishna tells Arjuna to let right deeds be his motive and not the fruit that comes from them. Can a person work for fruit in every season and still be free of concern for the fruit?
Jesus tells his disciples that when they have done all they were commanded they should say: we are unprofitable servants. How does that saying sit with the hope of becoming a tree laden with fruit?
Paul tells those who boast of the law that through their conduct the name of God is spoken against.

john-beareth-much-fruit.text: Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit; so shall ye be my disciples

john-he-purgeth-it.text: Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit

john-ordained-you.text: Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit should remain

psalm-fruit-in-old-age.text: The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon. Those that be planted in the house of the Lord shall flourish in the courts of our God. They shall still bring forth fruit in old age; they shall be fat and flourishing

matthew-good-ground.text: But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold

matthew-fig-tree-withered.text: And when he saw a fig tree in the way, he came to it, and found nothing thereon, but leaves only, and said unto it, Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever. And presently the fig tree withered away

luke-good-tree.text: For a good tree bringeth not forth corrupt fruit; neither doth a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit. For every tree is known by his own fruit. For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes. A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good; and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is evil: for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh

hebrews-peaceable-fruit.text: Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby

proverbs-fruit-of-the-righteous.text: The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise

hosea-sow-in-righteousness.text: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy; break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the Lord, till he come and rain righteousness upon you

hosea-sown-the-wind.text: For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind

corinthians-soweth-sparingly.text: But this I say, He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully

ecclesiastes-bread-upon-the-waters.text: Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days

isaiah-laboured-in-vain.text: Then I said, I have laboured in vain, I have spent my strength for nought, and in vain: yet surely my judgment is with the Lord, and my work with my God

james-fruit-of-righteousness.text: But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy. And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace

colossians-fruitful-in-every-good-work.text: That ye might walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing, being fruitful in every good work, and increasing in the knowledge of God

matthew-well-done.text: His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord

psalm-teach-us-to-number.text: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom

quran-seed-that-sendeth-forth.text: and their likeness in the Gospel - like as sown corn that sendeth forth its shoot and strengtheneth it and riseth firm upon its stalk, delighting the sowers

marcus-vine-which-has-produced-grapes.text: A third in a manner does not even know what he has done, but he is like a vine which has produced grapes, and seeks for nothing more after it has once produced its proper fruit
marcus-vine-which-has-produced-grapes.author: Marcus Aurelius

kant-like-a-jewel.text: if with its greatest efforts it should yet achieve nothing, and there should remain only the good will (not, to be sure, a mere wish, but the summoning of all means in our power), then, like a jewel, it would still shine by its own light, as a thing which has its whole value in itself. Its usefulness or fruitfulness can neither add nor take away anything from this value
kant-like-a-jewel.author: Immanuel Kant
kant-like-a-jewel.work: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals

mencius-man-of-song.text: There was a man of Song, who was grieved that his growing corn was not longer, and so he pulled it up. Having done this, he returned home, looking very stupid, and said to his people, "I am tired to-day. I have been helping the corn to grow long." His son ran to look at it, and found the corn all withered
mencius-man-of-song.author: Mencius
